lore: Eyestalkers are a very rare sighting in the Mist of Scales. They are distantly related to Mist Stalkers, but larger and even more aggressive. Rumors say that they are the result of a magical experiment by a Lamia to turn Mist Stalkers into an elite force that could guard her queen.

If that is the case, the Lamia certainly got the part of the spell right allowing Eyestalkers to be hyper-aware of their surroundings. Their eyes are large, extremely effective, and able to twist and turn at all angles. It is almost impossible to sneak up on one.

Some Naga mystics believe the eyes of an Eyestalker hold very powerful magical properties. They claim the vitreous fluid inside can be distilled to create a potion that allows a creature to see great detail at even greater distances. The fact that it is so highly prized has probably contributed to the scarcity of these misshapen creatures.

lore: Undead Armies have a natural advantage - their troops serve a multitude of purposes. It’s very nice when your infantry can be recycled not only as building materials for your siege weapons, but also as ammunition for those very same weapons.

The first Bone Catapult was created by the Gray King himself as he lay siege to the outer keeps of Sword’s Edge. As he marched westward, he would throw his army against a keep’s walls to overwhelm the defenders, then raise the dead from that castle as a new army, while turning his losses into bone catapults for the next siege.

This tactic almost allowed him to conquer the entirety of Sword’s Edge. Had it not been for a spirited defense from the Griffon Knights, he may well have triumphed. Nevertheless, the Bone Catapult has been a staple in the armies of Ghulvania ever since.

lore: Mydnight is home to many strange characters and creatures, each with unique and disturbing stories to tell. The Lady of Ruin’s is one of the strangest though. She tried to escape the city many centuries ago by making a pact with a Fey Lord who identified himself only as the Wyrm of Shadows. Pacts made with the Fey can be very dangerous though…

Originally known by the name Alvira, one night, having fallen into despair at being trapped within Mydnight, she summoned a Fey from the Dark Court and told it she wished to escape. It had a simple proposal: Bring me the soul of a child, and I will set you free of this place. Desperate, she did as requested, and the Fey cast her out of the city, but into the void between worlds.

There she remained, tormented for a decade, until the creature visited her once more. “One more soul”, it asked her, and I will consider your freedom. Predictably then, over the centuries, this murderous pact played out time and again. Alvira came to be known as the Lady of Ruin, since her arrival in Mydnight would herald the death of a child. And somewhere, in the Dark Court, a Fey known as the Shadow Wyrm grew more powerful.

lore: When the Mydnight Queen took control of the Kingdom of Mydnight, she warped all the creatures therein to conform to her ideals of perfection. She even altered the King’s Hounds, changing them from huge muscular beasts to emotionless skeletal shadows of their former selves.

One thing they never lost was their hunger. Eternally hungry, but no longer able to satisfy that craving, they became wilder and more ravenous as the years wore on. On occasion, their raspy howling would become so annoying that the Queen would simply let them loose among the people of her kingdom.

Most would return from these hunts, their loyalty as frozen in time as the Kingdom of Mydnight. But some would not - hiding on the edges of the Kingdom where time was fluid and ever-changing, catching any travelers as they passed by Mydnight’s latest location.

lore: Many years ago, the three Goblin scoundrels, Murk, Lurk, and Durk, were doing some… business… in Sword’s Edge when they came upon an object so unthinkable, so creative, so wondrous, that they knew they must immediately have it. At the stroke of midnight, they snuck into Falstaff’s Fantastical Fashion Emporium, and liberated this most unusual magical artifact… a trenchcoat.

Their thinking was simple. Goblins had always been looked down upon - it made it hard to complete a shady deal when most tallfolk realized that your eyes were about the same height as their moneypouch. But if they all climbed into The Trenchcoat of Power, then they would be the equal of any human, and in fact, even MORE trustworthy than a Dwarf!

When Murk, Lurk, and Durk returned to Zaejin they were rich. It wasn’t that people started believing their scams exactly, but The Trenchcoat of Power DID allow them to get close enough to targets so that Durk (on the bottom) could sneak a hand out between the buttons and help himself to those moneypouches.

lore: Sir Ailuin leads the Crystal Knights of Silverglade, an elite unit who guard the caves of the Crystal Dragons. When one thinks of Dragons in Silverglade, one usually thinks of Krystenax, but there are so many more than that. From the tiny Silver Drakons, up to their much larger and shinier cousins, they live with Krystenax in caves close to the palace.

Sir Ailuin is descended from a long line of Crystal Knights, and has guarded Krystenax’s extended family for over a century. He takes a special interest in protecting their eggs. Dragon eggs can take decades to hatch, and are extremely vulnerable to predators and thieves. Many times Sir Ailuin has saved them, and over the years has built up a strong bond with the Dragons.

He has, with his dedication, won back honor for his family. Sir Ailuin’s grandfather once failed in his task, and 7 eggs were stolen. Krystenax’s offspring were taken by an evil Sorcerer from Karakoth who turned his children into the fercious beasts Amethelias, Diamantina, Emeraldrin, Garnetaerlin,  Rubirath, Sapphirax, and Topasarth, who broke free to terrorize the world. Today they have been driven underground, and can be found deep within dungeons throughout Krystara.

lore: King Triton of Merlantis is a wise and noble leader of his people, much beloved by all the Merfolk. But like all wise and noble leaders, he has accumulated many enemies over the years. The Triton Guard are a hand-picked group of warriors who attend to the King all day, every day; one does not rule for centuries without a little healthy paranoia…

Mera joined the Triton Guard at a very young age. Like many young Merfolk of common birth, she aspired to become one of the guards, as it would bring both her and her family much honor. From the moment she could pick up a trident, she would practice her forms for hours out in the open waters, and all the practice finally paid off.

By chance, Terranaeus, the Captain of the Triton Guard, saw her practicing alone one day. He quickly organized to bring her before the Guard Council, and they unanimously voted for her to join. Within just four years, she was awarded the honor of wielding a golden Ocean Trident, marking her as one of their elite warriors at just 20 years of age.

lore: The Iron Maiden is the infamous captain of the blighted ship - The Infernal Voyager. She has served in the naval forces of the Infernal King’s blighted army for many centuries, and led them to many victories over Darkstone, the Leonis Empire, and Grosh-Nak.

In her early battles against Grosh-Nak, she captained an armada of burning vessels from the helm of the Fiery Seahawk, to smash into Grosh-Nak’s inadequate navy, destroying them all in the process, but bringing Grosh-Nak to its knees. Soon after, her King commissioned The Infernal Voyager as a reward for her leadership.

While technically still a part of the Blighted Fleet, her work today takes her further afield as a privateer - raiding merchants for the Infernal King. Many a sailor has soiled his breeches when he’s spied the burning hull of The Infernal Voyager on the horizon, and realized The Iron Maiden was coming for him.

lore: Prince Basalt is one of the royal family of Nexus. He is the son of Queen Ashe and King Heliodor, and the brother of Princess Shayle. Nevertheless, he is an accomplished warrior, and all believe that one day he will be a great leader.

Like all those Born of Stone, Prince Basalt is in the ruling caste. The Stoneborn are the nobles of Nexus, whereas the Waterborn are the religious caste, the Fireborn are the warrior caste. And although the Natureborn are the worker caste, Prince Basalt has often argued that they are the most important ones - the glue who hold all of Nexus together.

Given Prince Basalt’s ties to and love for the Natureborn, it is no surprise that he was a great supporter of the relationship between his sister, Princess Shayle, and the Natureborn Warden, Hawthorn. Unfortunately though, he did not give her a proper show of support when she needed it, but has vowed to make amends as he serves his Kingdom in the future.

lore: Long before it became known as Hellcrag, the city of Zhand was home to many different creatures, not least amongst those were the Fey, who lived in a grove outside the eastern gates, surrounded by Treants. They were generally on good terms with the sisters who ruled the city.

As the city fell to the Daemons, and Medusa enacted the Curse of Stone, the Fey were quick to escape; they already lived outside of the walls, and were able to get beyond the radius of the curse. The Treants were slow though, and they barely had time to move beyond their circle as their trunks and leaves were petrified.

As the centuries passed, the Treants gradually regained some movement - even more now that the curse has been lifted. Some of them have passed back over the seas to the Bright Forest, but many more have remained to help rebuild Hellcrag, and perhaps, in time, restore the city of Zhand.

lore: Sea Hags are a constant threat for ships heading to Darkstone. Fortunately, few folk with good intentions ever travel there, so there is a certain sense of justice in the fact that Krystara is generally better off without them. The Sea Hags, for all intents and purposes, do seem to perform a vital function in reducing the number of scumbags traveling the seas.

Typically, the first sign of a Sea Hag attack involves a ship being becalmed around 50 miles off Darkstone’s coast - the ocean becomes flat and the wind stops blowing. The Sea Hags then use their Tidal Curse to drift the ship towards their coven where they can rise up and pull the sailors from the decks, drowning them.

The Lords of Darkstone, tired of having their illicit trade disrupted, have tried to exterminate the Sea Hags more than once, but they have strong ties with other covens of hags on Darkstone. When the Darkstone War Galleys arrive, the Sea Hags are inevitably nowhere to be found. But when they head back to port, one or two will mysteriously vanish…

lore: In the times before the Curse of Stone, the Panthers of Zhand, now known as Hellcrag, were revered by the people for their grace, power, and beauty. They were sentient creatures and often worked with the folk of Zhand to defend their kingdom.

When the Curse was cast on Zhand by Medusa, it was not only the city that was affected. All manner of creatures in the surrounding lands were also caught up in the massive petrification that took place, and then slowly gained sentience over the centuries. This included the panthers.

Today the panthers have adapted to their new forms. Once again, they are defenders of their kingdom, though it is now called Hellcrag, leaping through the craggy peaks surrounding the central city, and swiping rocks down upon any invading forces.

lore: Huntmaster Arborius is a renowned Dragonian hunter and tracker from Dragon’s Claw. His simple green scales prove useful for camouflage, particularly as he often hunts in the Mist of Scales, but once he has engaged his prey, his scales shine red as he fixes his sights upon them.

Huntmaster Arborius’ bow is magical. It was acquired from a winged naga whom he battled in the swamp for a full week. Finally the naga was taken down, and offered up its bow in exchange for its life. This bow shoots magical arrows with wings on them that adjust their path to hit a target. To Arborius, they have always looked like Dragon wings.

Huntmaster Arborius’ companion is a Cobalt Drake he rescued from some Orcish poachers many years ago. Together, they often guide travelers on paths through Dragon’s Claw, helping them to avoid contact with the Dragonians, who can be a decidedly prickly bunch. His fees are exorbitant, but his knowledge of hidden paths and ravines is legendary

lore: Nobody is sure exactly where Jeweled Golems come from, but they are unique to Broken Spire. They are not Dwarven, nor are they Elven, Fey, or Daemonic in origin. Certainly, unsophisticated creatures like Infernus could not have created them. The mages of Karakoth have a theory they may be of Eldritch design though.

Just as their origin is unclear, so is their purpose. It is clear they prefer to find something to guard, but failing that, they will wander the crags and caverns of Broken Spire aimlessly, murdering anyone they meet. Perhaps in an age long past, they guarded something of note that has been lost, and they are still looking for it.

A few aspiring nobles and wizards have managed to capture a Jeweled Golem and set it to guarding their most prized treasures. It is remarkably effective, except that the Jeweled Golems will also try to stop the treasures’ owners from accessing their wealth. They are extremely dangerous, but also promote good saving and spending habits.

lore: Goblins are stereotypically nasty, vicious,and sly little creatures. The merchant, Slughoarder, takes that to a new level by adding unhealthy doses of covetousness and treachery. They say that he would sell his mother for 10 gold. That’s not true - he already sold her for 3 gold when he was just a young gobling.

Most folk who cross his path come away poorer for the experience - literally. Tales abound of his epic exploits in the underhanded vending of worthless junk; one tale tells of the time he sold a shipment of rocks to the Dwarves of Khaziel, which was actually just a piece of paper attached to a pickaxe, which read: 1.  Walk outside, 2. Start Digging Dumb%$

Some people ask where his name came from. Did he ever actually hoard slugs? And if so, who did he sell them to? The answer is of course, yes. In one of his finest moments, he exploited his siblings by getting them (unpaid, mind you) to collect slugs for him for 2 years, at which point he sold the slugs AND siblings to the Troll Queen Sycorax as delicacies for a huge feast.

lore: There’s very little loyalty amongst the pirates of Blackhawk - crew change ships often, as both pay, and vacancies (many caused by walking the plank) dictate. One crew member who has never been short of work is simply known as Boatswain Bart.

Bart is a navigator extraordinaire. His abilities to navigate precisely through many of the reefs around Blackhawk and off the mainland coasts near the Pridelands has saved the life of his crew many times. Even at night he has the uncanny knack of sailing by the stars.

Many folk have asked Bart if he wants to captain his own ship. ‘Maybe one day’ is his only response - he’s a man of few words. For now he seems content to learn every inch of coastline from Silverglade to the Leonis Empire and beyond.

lore: Having recently been led to believe she would bring about the end of the Spirit Talkers, Harper is understandably anxious about her place in the world. Despite being the supposed bringer of horrible fortune, she is well-liked among the fox-folk of Vulpacea.

Harper has been playing the lyre since she was a young kit, and is adamant that it is a distinct skill from playing the harp, because for her to play the harp would be a little too obvious. Her mother, who still frequently boasts about Harper’s ‘harp playing skills’, is annoyed by this fact.

Though Harper is now able to speak to spirits, she prefers to communicate with them through her lullabies. They allow her to convey complex emotions with the twang of her lute strings, and are often accompanied by simplistic lyrics.

lore: The Urska are, for the most part, a lovely people - family oriented, friendly to well-intentioned strangers, and simply desiring to get on with their lives in peace. Unfortunately, they live in one of the most inhospitable parts of Krystara, where some days, everything wants to kill you. It was from this fact that the Spirit of Rage was born.

When the peaceful folk of Urskaya begin to grow angry, that anger manifests itself as a large red and black bear with angry red crystals protruding from its flesh. The Spirit of Rage seems to innately understand the target of the anger and sets out on a mission of blind hatred.

As a defense mechanism, the Spirit of Rage has been very successful. If harming the Urska results in tenfold destruction visited back upon you, then you tend to leave them alone. Sadly though, this means most folk shy away from interacting withe the Urska at all, simple for fear of accidentally angering some of them.

lore: While the Gladewardens form the first line of defense in the Forest of Thorns, it is the Thorn Scouts who exist out beyond that line, gathering intelligence on any threats to the forest. Wood Elves may move silently through the trees, but the Thorn Scouts are an elite group, who make less noise than a shadow in the moonlight.

Thorn Scouts will often be deployed within their homelands to assess a new threat before heavier troops are sent in. If caught off guard, they are also more than capable warriors, wielding twin daggers made of iron oak, and entwined with the thorns of the obsidian rose plant.

Beyond the borders of the Forest of Thorns, they can also be found in Whitehelm, Karakoth, Khetar, the Mist of Scales, and Grosh-Nak, where they often undertake secret missions for the Wood Elf Lords, in attempts to preemptively upset any nefarious plans by the rulers of those rival realms. Wood Elves may seem a fair and generous folk, but the Thorn Scouts are neither of those things when their kingdom is threatened.

lore: The Animus of Envy began her existence as the daughter of an ancient king, raised in luxury yet consumed by the belief that her older brother had more of everything. Her jealousy grew so fierce that she murdered him in a fit of rage, a crime that led to her execution. As she died, the Daemon Lord Envy appeared, delighted by her spite, and carried her into the Sin of Maraj to shape her into his lieutenant.

She inspires envy so potent that it corrodes friendships, kingdoms, and family reunions. With a whisper she can turn admiration into bitterness, and with a glance she can make a contented soul crave what it never wanted before. Even among daemons she is notorious for resenting anyone who has more, including her own master. It is even said she invented the board game ‘Diplomacy’.

It is said she was there at the fall of Ancient Khet, when she slipped into the royal court and convinced every noble that their neighbour’s wealth was stolen from them. The resulting chaos toppled the kingdom in a single night, which she considered a personal triumph. To this day she wanders the realms, seeding envy wherever she goes, forever jealous of anyone who seems even slightly happier than she is.

lore: The first reported sighting of a Living Quartz being was believed to be a hoax made up by a Dwarven Miner trying to bring some excitement to his workplace. Opinions quickly changed when that same Living Quartz broke half the mining equipment.

For a brief time, the Dwarves considered trying to mine ore from the backs of the Living Quartz, but eventually they came to their senses and realized they wouldn’t enjoy it if someone chipped away at little bits of their bodies. A few unscrupulous ones still try though.

Living Quartz are actually quite patient beings, and are aware that a few miners may attempt to take ore from their backs. Dwarves have often said there is a ‘three strikes and you’re out’ rule - if you strike a Living Quartz three times, it will grab you and rip you apart!

lore: Wererats inhabit both urban and rural areas, feeding off the dregs and offcuts left behind by the more civilized races. They are scavengers by nature, but when the opportunity presents itself they have no qualms about resorting to thievery.

When in giant rat form, Wererats can often be seen swarming the sewers and opting for safety in numbers. In their humanoid form, however, they will usually dart through the shadows alone, finding it easier to travel the world undetected.

Though not naturally inclined to help those in need, a Wererat’s loyalty can be temporarily bought. Just don’t expect them to do more than explicitly asked of them, and definitely don’t expect a job done by a Wererat (or two) to be done elegantly.

lore: Grimmoira was once a Fey child abandoned and left to die by cruel parents in the Glacial Peaks. Fortunately, she was found by the sage, Tassarion, who took her in and raised her as one of his own.

She became Tassarion’s student, where she excelled at learning, with an almost eidetic memory for the books she read. Soon Tassarion came to rely on her wide knowledge, and being the old curmudgeon that he is, would often consult Grimmoira, and then claim the facts or conclusions as his own.

Still, Grimmoira is grateful to Tassarion for saving her life, and while she detests his rudeness and arrogance, she is loyal to a fault. In later years, she has become his personal librarian, managing his legendary collection of tomes and scrolls in his secret library in the Glacial Peaks.

lore: Ulf Harrigan began his life in the humble quarters of the Swords Edge city guard, where he learned discipline, patience, and how to avoid being trampled by horses. Through grit and talent he rose into the ranks of the Wolf Knights, a fearsome order famed for their crossbow accuracy and axe work. By the time he became Knight Commander, he could shoot, strike, and dodge a horse in a single motion.

With his roguish wolf-like countenance, Ulf is so strikingly handsome that mirrors have been known to blush, apologise, and quietly fog themselves up out of sheer embarrassment. He is also careful, clever, and always three steps ahead in battle, which is why the Wolf Knights follow his orders without hesitation. His only flaw is his fondness for the ladies, though he insists it never distracts him from duty.

During the Siege of the Ironwood Gate, when a surprise attack threatened to overwhelm the defenders, Ulf rallied the Wolf Knights, coordinated a flawless counterstrike, and personally held the breach long enough for reinforcements to arrive. Queen Ysabelle herself commended him afterward, though several noblewomen also sent him admiring letters, which he very responsibly ignored until the kingdom was safe again.

lore: Soldiers of the Lord of Envy, these Daemonic maidens are so destined to become beacons of jealousy that they are literally born green. Obviously, that leaves them jealous of the beautiful fiery skin of other Daemons, which turns them greener still.

The Maids of Envy were tasked with guarding a piece of the Ancient Maraji Crown, but sadly lost it to the Emperor Khorvash in his campaign to reclaim the Leonine throne. That saw them relegated to simple foot-soldiers of Envy, which - as you might guess - leaves them even greener.

Today, the Maids of Envy are looking for a way back into their Lord’s good graces. As you might imagine, they are desperately jealous of all those above them in the hierarchy, and that makes them dangerous indeed.

lore: This should not be confused with a Dark GIN Bottle, even though the contents of either can leave you incapacitated. No, this particular Djinn Bottle contains a spirit of a very different kind - either a Djinn, Ifrit, or Dao from the old Maraji Empire. They may be called forth from the bottle by rubbing it.

Legends say that any creature summed from such a bottle owes you three wishes, but that isn’t quite true - it depends on the spell binding the creature there. Some may certainly grant wishes within their powers, but others may be bound to protect you from harm 3 times, or even to DO harm to you three times.

Fortunately most of the summoned Djinn, Ifrit, and Dao are friendly and will perform their task in a good natured fashion, then depart back into the bottle which will immediately disappear, only to appear miles away, awaiting their new owner.

lore: The hierarchies of the Fey are deep, twisted, and complex. This is true of the Wild Court, the Dark Court, the Winter Court, and especially the Summer Court. The Spring Emissary is a prime example of this complexity. Who does she represent? Where do her alliances lie? It is difficult to say.

One thing is certain though, the Spring Emissary is a repository of knowledge. She knows everyone’s business in the Summer Court, and is often used as a first point of contact between two parties to settle a dispute or arrange a meeting.

Being the Spring Emissary, she is also accustomed to liaising with the Winter Court, just as with the seasons, Spring is between Summer and Winter. But it has led many of the Fey to question - could there be a secret Spring Court that they do not know about?

lore: The people of Krystara often think of the Infernal King when they think of a Daemonic Lord - mainly because he led the Blight that infested the southern lands long ago. Although many more powerful Daemons may have come and gone from Krystara, the Infernal King’s influence is burned into the history books. Few ever consider Baphomet as a great leader though - perhaps foolishly.

Baphomet’s lineage is entirely different to the Infernal King - there is a touch of the divine about his many legged form; and there is also a cold level of cunning and wisdom that the Infernal King never possessed. Baphomet has designs on starting another Blight, but he is not driven by the same impetuous whims as his kin.

Baphomet has, in fact, traveled to Krystara on numerous occasions, but not as a general - not yet anyway. He has rampaged around the world, learning about the landscapes, the peoples, their strengths, and their weaknesses. Should the next Blight ever begin, and should Baphomet be leading it, Krystara must beware.

lore: Sir Alamir is the current leader of the Knights of the Burning Axe, and a descendant of the Undead Knight. the Watchman of Khetar, Sir Alastair. Like his ancestor, Sir Alamir is a masterful warrior, and a great leader who takes his responsibilities seriously.

The Knights of the Burning Axe are one of the oldest orders of Knighthood in Whitehelm. Originally formed to repel a Frost Giant invasion long ago, they eventually found their place protecting the borders of Whitehelm from Khetari Undead.

Each Knight, like Sir Alamir, carries a large two-handed axe. In battle they pray to Gard to ignite their axe, and if they have been true to their oath, the axe will flare up with a massive burst of searing holy fire that both Undead and creatures of frost have grown to fear.

lore: There are many types of bats in Krystara, particularly in the kingdom of Ghulvania, but one breed stands out in many ways - the Doombat. Not only is its midnight and crimson color quite striking, but its wingspan stretches over 3 meters. What is most memorable about the Doombat though are the myths and legends associated with it.

Known for their endurance, Doombats range far and wide from their deep caves in Ghulvania. They are considered by most folk to be a sign of ill omen. Many villagers will ward their doors and windows with protective charms made of silver and moonstone to keep them away. If they do appear though, their distinctive cry announces them, it is thought by many to herald a death in the family.

Much of the fear of Doombats possibly stems from the Great Krystaran Plague, many centuries ago - the first recorded sighting of a Doombat coincided with the beginning of the plague. After that, they were hunted, nearly to extinction. Had it not been for their ability to shadowmeld and hide, they may indeed have been wiped out. Some folk even believe the horrors they now visit are revenge for that culling.

lore: Crysturtles live alongside the Merfolk of Merlantis in peaceful harmony, and have long enjoyed a relationship built on mutual respect. The Merpeople defend the reef, keeping all who live there safe, and the Crysturtles act as living artworks, their shiny backs inspiring awe in those who pass them by.

Not all Crysturtles are adorned with crystals of the same color - they come in all hues and combinations of the rainbow, and a Crysturtle’s crystal color may change over the course of its lifetime. There are benefits to all shades, as some may be more well-known for their beauty, while others are better at camouflaging with their environment.

The love for Crysturtles is so strong in some Merfolk that they have formed groups that organize Crysturtle-watching expeditions. They like to let people know that they think these magnificent creatures are ‘Crys-turtally awesome’.

lore: Sir Robert the Resolute was a terrible knight. The only thing lower than his standards was his intelligence. People often joked that his horse was smarter than him. Unfortunately they were right - so right that even the horse knew it. One day, as Sir Robert was riding home from another unsuccessful quest, trying to pick his nose through his visor with his longsword, his horse threw him and ran off.

Sir Robert’s tale ends there, impaled through the cribriform plate with his own weapon. His horse however, moved on to greater things. Now free, and searching for a purpose, it discovered the Divinion Fields. A lush green land, filled with Centaurs who welcomed him.

Grateful for his new life, Sir Robert’s horse resolved to protect its new home. Whenever a threat arose anywhere in the Divinion Fields, it would show up in full armor, ready for battle. Over time, the Centaurs referred to it as the Guardian of the Fields.

lore: Deep within the dark borders of Ghulvania lives a depraved vampiric lord known as Vlad the Unsated. Originally just a villager in one of the small huddled Ghulvanian towns, Vlad rose to power after discovering an ancient cup belonging to worshippers of the Crimson Bat., It was known as the Chalice of Vampiric Thirst. Of course Vlad wasn’t aware of that at the time.

Vlad knew the chalice was magical, however, and he toyed with it for many weeks before deciding to drink from it. The pain it inflicted upon him was extreme as his body began to change from human to something resembling a strange humanoid bat. And that was when the hunger began.

Once the curse of Vampiric Thirst gripped Vlad, he couldn’t stop. Within a week, he had lured dozens of other townsfolk to his house, and drained them dry. He discovered with each one, his strength grew, and so over time, he seized control of his home village, then the villages nearby, and finally the castle of the lord who presided over them all. And still he was hungry...

lore: The Scarabi are the rarest of the scorpions found in the Drifting Sands, but their blue crystalline chitinous plates and their twin tails make them very easy to spot. It’s just as well they’re rare too, as the only thing worse than a giant scorpion, is a giant scorpion with TWO stingers!

The Scarabi are prized trophies from a hunt, and every part of the creature is put to use. Although large, their meat is considered a delicacy. And their crystalline skin is used to craft the finest armor.

Finally, the poison is extremely deadly, and the Sisterhood of Darkness on Darkstone are known to pay extremely well for any that is gathered. All that said, they are not endangered; their apparent rarity is mainly due to the fact that those who see them often never live to report the sighting.

lore: The landscapes of the Daemon Realms vary as much as the landscapes of Krystara. Not all of them are broken and burning hellpits wreathed in sulfurous fumes. Similarly, not all Daemons are fiery - some, like Ba’el, are covered in slime.

Ba’el hails from the Daemon Realm of Brzgudlotrull - the Realm of Slime. Here all manner of foul Daemonic creatures crawl around in the fetid muck, feeding on each other. Some are formless, but many more are like great slimy reptiles and amphibians.

Ba’el was summoned from this morass by a coven of Sea Hags on the Isle of Darkstone. Ba’el was fast - he had been both predator and prey in his home realm, but had been difficult to catch. Before the hags could bind him, he leapt away and bounded off into the night. He still roams the shores of Darkstone to this day.

lore: Qilins live in the high peaks of Shentang, where the Sky Elves believe that the clouds themselves shaped its body from drifting mist and dragon fire. It grew into a creature of quiet majesty, half horse, mostly dragon, and entirely confusing to anyone who preferred life to stay predictable. From the moment they first appeared, people whispered that a Qilin’s presence meant change was coming.

Qilins can sense the turning of fate, which they acknowledge with gentle snorts and encourage with the occasional spark of celestial flame. This talent makes them beloved by philosophers and absolutely loathed by kings who fear anything that might rearrange their schedules. The Qilin, for its own part, remains baffled that mortals cannot decide whether to welcome it with garlands of flowers or chase it away with pointy sticks.

For this reason, Qilins prefer to live among the everchanging clouds - the sky offers peace, quiet, and far fewer people waving swords at them. They spend their days drifting between mountaintops, watching the world below shift and shuffle like a very slow board game, napping in sunbeams and just occasionally practicing a mysterious I’m-gonna-change-your-world ‘smoulder’ for the next time someone spots them.

lore: Most Raksha are fiercely loyal to their clans and families, but every rule has its exceptions. While many Raksha will undertake a quest to travel out into the Pridelands and slay the fiercest creature they can manage, some keep traveling - they are known as Free-Bloods.

The term Free-Blood is often used as an insult amongst Raksha to question another’s loyalty. This is because the Free-Bloods seldom return. Often they work abroad as very effective mercenaries, using the power their cat-like ferocity has gifted them with.

It is not unusual, when hiring a mercenary band, to find one or two Free-Bloods amongst its members. As might be expected, their attitudes differ widely; some regret their choice and wish they could return home, while others bask in all the world of Krystara has to offer.

lore: Taloca is one of the princes of Suncrest, a child of Garuda, but estranged from the royal family and no longer using his royal title. Part of the reason for this involves him shunning the fiery powers of his father to follow his own path among the Strygiks, and learn the power of lightning.

Taloca may have begun his stormy lightning-journey with the Strygiks (owl-like Stryx who are wise masters of the storm), but it did not end there. He progressed to learn more from the Stormsinger himself - master of ALL storms, not just lightning. And even secret knowledge from the reclusive Ehcatl.

As a result Taloca was able to use the might of ANY storm to augment the power of his own lightning, leaving him perhaps the strongest of the Sons of Gardua, and yet the least likely to eventually vie for the throne.

lore: Goblins get everywhere. You can’t travel anywhere in Krystara without finding some local variation on a Goblin. They share various traits in common though - they are universally fidgety, violent, unhinged, hungry, cunning, and always slightly peeved about something that’s actually too small for most sane folk to care about. Ice Goblins are all of those things… and blue.

While Ice Goblins can be found all throughout the north of Krystara, you are most likely to find them in the abandoned mines of Dhrak-Zum. Here, their incredible tolerance for cold (and each other’s company) has allowed them to create a business blowing up the living ice crystals in the mines and selling their fragments to sketchy wizards.

Like all Goblins, they are harmless if encountered by themselves. Also, like all Goblins, they are seldom ever encountered by themselves, as they prefer to move in murderous packs of 20 or more. If they catch you alone, you’re pretty much doomed, unless you look like you have absolutely nothing worth stealing.

lore: The Spiritdancers of Maugrim Woods are powerful and talented oracles. They seek guidance from their ancestors by calling and conversing with Spirit Foxes, a rarely-sighted magical beast in the woods that exists half in this plane and half within the realm of spirits. The Spirit Foxes speak a strange language only the Spiritdancers seem to understand.

The tradition of Spiritdancing originates in Vulpacea where the fox-folk converse freely with the spirit world on a regular basis. In Vulpacea, it is more a performance, and less of a magical ritual though. For the fox-folk of Maugrim Woods, who are less talented in the magical arts, Spiritdancing is the only practical way they have of talking with the spirits.

The dances performed are long and intricate - a clear sign of their performative origins. At the end of such a dance, which can last well over half an hour, the Spiritdancer will fall prone from exhaustion and if the ritual was successful, a small Spirit Fox will appear, sitting upon their chest and whispering in their ear.

lore: The most deadly Naga are often not the warriors. Fortunately for the rest of us, the charming and mesmerizing powers of the Naga are somewhat unreliable, and often a little hit-and-miss. Viper, however, has honed her powers of mind control with fine precision… she’s less hit-and-miss, and more hiss-and-kiss.

One famous tale tells of a mercenary band who thought hiring her was clever. By dawn, the mercenaries were gone, replaced by a suspicious number of very well-fed snakes sunning themselves on the rocks. The only survivor claimed he escaped because Viper said his breath was worse than a crocolisk who’d eaten a week-old skunk carcass.

After years of charm, theft, and lies, Viper eventually murdered her way to a position of power in the Royal Naga Court. Anyone who stood in her way tended to stop standing altogether - it was messy. But today, she can mostly be found entertaining foreign dignitaries in the most elaborate fashion, while deciding which ones to snack on later.

lore: Willow is an ancient elemental spirit - as old as the forest of Silverglade itself. She traveled amongst the forest’s whispering trees as they first grew, learning their innermost secrets. Sadly, she never spent an equal amount of time amongst the High Elves, so she cannot converse with them (even if the Dwarves do, rather unkindly, believe that Elves and trees are closely related).

Most of Willow’s kind vanished long ago, leaving her to patrol the woods with only the Florafawns and suspicious mushrooms for company. Fortunately, she can rouse ancient trees from their naps for a quick gossip, though more often it is to convince them to swat some goblins, or skewer a cheeky Dwarf. She leaves Elves alone for the most part though.

Still, it would be a mistake to underestimate Willow as a remnant of the past… When the Blight Wolves crept into Silverglade, she summoned a grove of angry birches and led them on a thunderous charge. The wolves were tangled, trampled, and politely composted before the Elves had finished stringing their bows. But when the High Elven King tried to thank his new allies, he was sent packing by a bunch of unruly birches that left him looking like he’d just endured an epic session in an Urskayan sauna.

lore: Chief Stronghorn was born into a family where leadership was less a career choice and more a hereditary mandate. His parents named him Chief because they assumed he would grow into the role, and to be fair, he did, though not without a few misunderstandings along the way; for example, anyone who ever mistakenly called him Keith has not lived long enough to repeat the mistake.

Horn-care is his passion, which he treats with the seriousness of a sacred rite and the focus of someone polishing for posterity. Each morning he applies lacquer with careful precision, knowing that shiny horns strike fear into enemies and impress potential bards. The tribe pretends not to notice how long this takes, mostly because they value their ribs unbroken.

All that horn-maintenance has a reason though. Chief Stronghorn has been waiting for his defining moment for years, convinced that fate will eventually present something suitably dramatic, like his father Steel Stronghorn who ripped open a fortress gate with his own gleaming horns, or his grandfather Thrust Stronghorn, who once skewered a Red Dragon with his one remaining, yet legendarily magnificent, horn.

lore: There is a well-known children’s rhyme which serves as a warning about Bulettes: I found tracks, but much to my sorrow,, They were not ones I ever would follow, ‘Cause to fight a Bulette, It’s Urskayan Roulette, If it bites, there’s a chance it might swallow.

Indeed, Bulettes are fearsome creatures. Fortunately, they are seldom found outside the Wild Plains, where they will typically burrow in amongst some rocks, then wait for a creature to pass by. They are fast, in short bursts, and can quickly take down something as large as a Minotaur, even swallowing it whole!

Tauros will often band together, hunting a Bulette, as they are considered a delicacy. Typically they will try to find some creature to use as bait then go looking for Bulette tracks with their bait in tow. Once the Bulette pounces, the Minotaurs will leap atop it with their axes. It’s not unusual to see Minotaurs missing a limb or two from a Bulette hunting incident.

lore: Deep in the Silver Forest, if you are paying very close attention, you might just catch a brief glimpse of a Hind. Not only are they incredibly fast and nimble, but their long flowing hair forms a remarkable camouflage in the undergrowth. Unfortunately, a glimpse of a Hind might also be the very last thing you see - they are powerful and formidable hunters.

Hinds live in small family herds of 15 to 20 creatures, but frequently meet up with other herds at seasonal gatherings four times per year. These gatherings, known as Quarterfests, can attract hundreds, if not thousands, of the creatures. They run for almost a week, and the reveling can become quite wild.

Between times though, Hinds are seldom seen, even by the sharp eyes of the High Elves. By day, the female hinds hunt, and the male hinds tend to their small hidden hobby farms. And by night, the herd will travel from one hunting ground to the next, before sleeping, and doing it all over again.

lore: Like many of the Sky Elves of Shentang, Spellblades - the main protectors of the hidden kingdom - are tall, lithe, and elegant. As their name suggests, not only are they competent warriors, but they are also conversant in magic. And they can fly!

In battle, the Spellblade will typically begin by imbuing their blade with a pulsing green light. As they swing it, not only does magic fire from the tip of the weapon, but the light grows, extending to enchant any allies standing nearby. A host of Spellblades side-by-side is a fearsome sight for any foe, as they all simultaneously light up and advance in unison.

In recent years, the Spellblades have been at the forefront of the battle against Yao Guai and his Daemon army. But after his defeat, there has been a quieter time where the Spellblades have been able to meditate on their situation and - once again - begin the process of Ascension, where they aim to leave the mortal world behind.

lore: The Leviathan comes from the deepest waters beyond the Blood Reef, where sea monsters once roamed in such numbers that even the sharks were polite. As food grew scarce the creatures turned on each other until only the Leviathan, a Giant Axolotl, and Donk the giant-lobster-with-a-man's-head remained. The Leviathan invited them to discuss survival, then ate them instead, which solved nothing except some short term hunger pangs.

Never one to plan ahead, the Leviathan did manage to cross Blood Reef, a feat no other monster had managed without being shredded, trapped, or very politely torn in two by the coral. The Leviathan pushed through with sheer stubbornness and an impressive lack of self care, emerging on the far side hungry enough to snack on anything that moved. It brought him into the waters near Merlantis, where Merfolk and Lamprey became his new favourite treats.

There was a decades-long effort by the Merfolk to drive him away from their kingdom. He would vanish for months at a time, ranging as far as the Broken Spire for some spicy take-out, only to return for a quick bite of whale or an unwary patrol when nobody was looking. Tales are unclear whether he was finally defeated for good, or just wandered off in search of dessert. Just in case, Merfolk keep a close eye out when they swim too far from home.

lore: It is customary for the Dwarven Crown of Khaziel to pass to the eldest child (male or female) of the previous monarch. However, the Highforge Dynasty had a dilemma; Old Queen Bronhilda Highforge II gave birth to twins. Ordinarily this wouldn’t have been an issue, as the firstborn twin would have received the Crown. BUT, due to the Dwarven midwife having to hasten to the royal chambers (after a long night playing drinking games at the tavern), there was an incident where she dropped both boys on their heads and mixed them up.

The Queen, in her wisdom, decided that since Dwarven Ale got them into this mess, it was only fitting that Dwarven Ale should get them out of it. So when the time came for the crown to pass to its new owner, she proclaimed a royal drinking contest to determine who should wear it. Prince Bardin Highforge went first. He drank 20 tankards of the strongest Dwarven Brew they could find, then threw his axe at a target on the wall and hit a bulls-eye. He turned to his twin brother and said, “Ha! Beat that, Grumdur, ye little worm!” He then burped, and fell on his face.

Prince Grumdur, left the hall, and was gone for a full hour before he returned, whereupon he gulped down 20 tankards, like his brother before him, grabbed his axe, threw it, and split his sibling’s axe in two, head and all. The crowd cheered, and Grumdur was proclaimed the new King! Queen Bronhilda was curious though, and she asked her son where he had gone for that hour before he drank the ale and threw the axe. “Well,” said the new King Grumdur Highforge, “It looked to be a tricky business, drinkin’ all that ale, and throwin’ axes… So I wanted to take a practice run first!”

lore: Queen Grapplepot rose to power in the goblin clans of Zaejin by being larger, louder, and far hungrier than any goblin before her. She grew to three times the size of a normal goblin, which is generally considered a sign of great leadership, great appetite, and great concern for those nearby. By the time she claimed the throne, most goblins had learned that disagreeing with her was a very quick way to become dinner.

She treasures her magical cauldron, and is a dedicated cook, though calling it cooking might be generous, since most of her ingredients come with a ‘Worst Before’ date on them. She stirs her bubbling pot day and night, tossing in deadly mushrooms, charred bones, old boots, and the occasional rude goblin who forgot to say please. The result is a stew so foul that even trolls refuse seconds, which only makes her prouder.

She once unveiled a dish so horrifying that half her clan fainted and the other half fled. She declared it a triumph and celebrated by throwing three unconscious guests into the pot for extra seasoning. To this day her clan obeys her every command, mostly because they prefer not to become part of the menu.

lore: In the Leonis Empire, falconry is a popular sport practised only by the nobility. Every noble of any note will have at least one or two Falconers in their employ, and quite possibly a stable of different birds, including Falcons, Hawks, Eagles, Owls, and Osprey, all well fed and cared for.

As such, a good Falconer is a highly-prized retainer. They work hard, but are extremely well-compensated for their skill and dedication to their birds. A Falconer’s day starts early, before their lords are even awake, training the younger birds. The day can also end late, as they ensure  all the birds are safe and well.  Many Falconers even sleep with the birds.

Like most important professions, they have their own Guild, which oversees the qualifications and certification of new Falconers. Young men and women constantly apply to the Guild for training, but positions are usually purchased by middle-class parents with bribes paid to the Guildmasters.

lore: King Mikhail rose to power in the frozen mountains of Urskaya, a land where the title of King goes to whoever is strong enough to take it and loud enough to insist they deserve it. He was not born into royalty, but he fought, roared, and punched his way to the top with the enthusiasm of a dragon that had just seen an unguarded pile of treasure. For more than a decade he has ruled with a booming voice, a bossy attitude, and a remarkable ability to make terrible decisions with absolute confidence.

King Mikhail is unnaturally strong; it’s the sort of strength that allows a person to walk across continents and tame creatures that most people only whisper about. As a young Urska he marched all the way to Zaejin, punched a Black Beast in the snout, and rode it home as if this were a perfectly normal thing to do. Since then he has added a Dragon, a Daemonic Goat, and a mid-sized offspring of the Ctharrasque to his stable, all of whom he subdued with his own fists and claws.

A visiting High Elf diplomat from Silverglade once asked to see King Mikhail’s legendary royal stables and fainted at the sight of the beasts inside. Mikhail proudly explained that any King worth their crown should have a stable that terrifies both enemies and allies alike. He then tossed the Elf in as dinner. Most folk now agree that they are just as frightened of what King Mikhail rides as they are of the King himself, which suits him just fine.

lore: Drakes are the flightless cousins of Dragons, and come in many types and sizes. They can be as large as the The Great Wyrm of Wyrmrun, or as small as the Simple Drake, known by most folk in Krystara as just the “Drake”. These smaller Drakes are very common, and can be found anywhere in the world.

In Grosh-Nak, these Drakes are prized as mounts amongst the Orcs. They are extremely violent, ill-tempered, and difficult to train, so it takes a creature of matching temperament to have a good chance at bringing them under control. This makes Orcs the  perfect companion for them, and given a young Drake, with one or two years of training, they can eventually be ridden into battle.

Once this bond has been established though, Drakes become incredibly loyal. If their rider is knocked down, it is not unusual to see the Drake standing over their body, protecting them. Most Orcs would leave them alone; as they know well, it’s not the bite of these smaller Drakes you need to watch out for, it’s the heavy tail slam that comes in from the side and shatters your spine!

lore: The two daughters of Orion - Artema and Anthea - are as different as night and day. Anthea is the younger daughter - a lover of nature, often seen running wild and free - while Artema is the older, always in search of battle.

Anthea enjoys the smell of the trees, and the feel of the long grass as it brushes against her fetlocks. Upon occasion, in Spring, she will visit small tribal villages, bearing herbal blooms and medicinal plants, which she gives away freely to all in need.

Artema thinks her foolish - she loves war instead. Seldom seen without a lance in her hands, the local tribes shy away from her, believing it is bad luck if she crosses their path. Unlike Anthea, when Artema enters your village, it is to recruit warriors, and they are seldom seen again!

lore: High in the mountains of Suncrest, the Stryx have built many fantastical monuments and temples. Some of those temples are dedicated to the Goddess of Dark Wisdom, Ixiquetacla, and it is here you will find the largest  gathering of the Owleth - every night they flock to these temples for a series of solemn ceremonies.

To see groups of Owleth chanting is an eerie sight, but even more eerie is to watch them leave, their eyes glowing blue and staring sightlessly ahead. During these ceremonies, their Goddess gifts them with fragmentary visions of the future, but only the dark and ominous parts that may occur.

As a consequence, the Owleth are prized for their Dark Omens. The Stryx royalty often keep Owleth around to warn them if there may be a dire consequence to an action they are taking. The problem is that there is very little one can do that doesn’t have a potential for a bad outcome. But the Stryx are a very conservative folk.

lore: The Forest Guardian was once a very rude wolf in the ancient lands of Elemaugrim, a creature who refused to join in a howl or play a friendly game of bitey-face. The ancestral wolf spirits grew tired of his unwolfly attitude and transformed him into a giant magical stag, giving him an important job to encourage better behavior. Eventually he joined them - an ancestral spirit in his own right.

As The Forest Guardian, he can rally the creatures of the woods, from wandering badgers to watchful owls, all bound by his quiet authority. Tales say he once stood beside Wulfgarok, the First Wargare, and together they slew the ancient Black Dragon Elemaugrim, clearing the land for the Wargare to build a kingdom and flourish. Some whisper that Wulfgarok himself may return to fight beside the guardian if the woods are ever truly threatened again.

The Forest Guardian still glances wistfully at wolves whenever they start a good howl though. He still hopes - against all odds - that if he is a good boy and protects the woods well enough, the ancestral spirits might one day reward him by turning him back into a wolf, preferably one allowed to skip bitey-face though.

lore: A phenomenon that only seems to occur in Karakoth is the Void Portal. Sages have theorized it is because the fabric of reality - the veil separating our plane with others - is weaker there. Why is the fabric weak in Karakoth? Is it all the eldritch summoning that took place millenia ago? Or were eldritch Daemons simply drawn there because the veil was weak in the first place.

When a void portal appears, it is quite a dramatic event. Rocks will thrust up from the ground like jagged teeth, and a swirling fiery portal will explode into place between them. Anyone who has witnessed this always comments that they feel a malevolent purpose at work. For this reason it is believed the portals may be actively created by Daemons from the other side.

The biggest problem with Void Portals is the creatures that sneak through into our plane. Smaller Imps frequently appear, and while they don’t pose much of a problem, it is their larger cousins that do. For that reason, even the most corrupt and vile sorcerers in Karakoth will generally take the time to close down any portal they find.

lore: The Dragon Knights are one of the noble orders of Knights from Sword’s Edge. Sadly, their order was betrayed by the Knights Coronet, as their leader, General Luther, sought out Sheggra’s Heart to heal his ailing queen.

Fortunately, General Luther was able to return to Sword’s Edge with the heart, then bring the Knights Coronet to justice, and begin the restoration of the Dragon Knights. Even now, their ranks swell with new recruits eager to wear the famed Dragon Helms as they serve the crown.

It is believed they obtained their name from General Ioetta the Tenacious. She founded the order many centuries ago, before even the splintering of the Adanian Empire. Ancient tapestries and texts show her riding a huge golden dragon.

lore: DRACOS-1337 was forged from the creative chaos of Sparkgrinder’s workshop where the Tinker Dwarf builds mechs that may be brilliant or catastrophic - or more likely both. This particular creation took the shape of a massive metal dragon - its name stands for ‘Draconic Robotic Assistant Courtesy of Sparkgrinder’. As for the number 1337, some say it is a random designation, while others whisper that it carries deep meaning in the secret language of the Tinker Dwarves.

DRACOS-1337 can blast things with lasers shot from its eyes. Sparkgrinder claims this is essential for keeping watch over Carnex, his earlier dog mech that once rampaged across Adana. However, many folk suspect it was just built as a new way to barbecue cats, since Sparkgrinder has very strong feelings about them. Whatever the truth, its short leaps combined with searing beams make it dangerous to everything from cats to Carnex to college professors, as you will see below.

Upon its completion, Sparkgrinder demonstrated its abilities to the Royal College of Engineers. He did this by firing a laser at them - not out of malice, but because he thought the college was in need of some repair anyway. It missed, slicing through a tree, a fence, the Dean of the College, and three cats, who Sparkgrinder insists had nothing to do with its aim being off by 157 degrees. Overall it was well-received - nobody liked the old Dean anyway, and three cats is a small price to pay for technological advancement.

lore: The Inquisitors of Whitehelm were established millennia ago, after Whitehelm’s split from the Empire of Adania, as a way to protect the church against corruption. Unfortunately, they have not always been as successful as their founders hoped.

So, 3 centuries past, the Grand Inquisitors were established - a group of vicious fanatics bent on rooting out corruption in their own order. Nicknamed the “Toe-Cutters” (for a reason), their motto has been “No matter how many innocent people die, no guilty man should go free”.

Unfortunately, history repeated itself with the rise of Moloch. This time the Grand Inquisitors were compromised, and had it not been for their unwarranted attacks on the lands of Lady Sapphira, and the timely intervention of our hero, the corruption may very well have spread through Whitehelm.

lore: The ancient Empire of Khet, long before it crumbled, was home to many cults. Two of the most powerful cults were the Anubites and the Settites, and they were always at war. The Anubites were a death cult, based around the worship of dead ancestors. Their priests created large jackal-like monstrosities to guard their tombs - the Anubite Warriors.

The Settites, on the other hand, worshiped nature in its many guises - in particular the gods of the rivers that brought life to Khet. It was the war between the Anubites and the Settites that eventually brought the entire Kingdom of Khet to its knees. The Anubites destroyed the Settites’ Rivers, creating a drought, and the Settites broke open the Anubites’ Tombs, unleashing a horde of Undead upon the world.

Today, all that remains of Khet’s former glory are the jagged ruins of Khetar, dry and dusty, its inhabitants long gone. The only life you will find here are the eternal creatures such as the Anubite Warriors who wander aimlessly through the pillaged tombs, still looking for enemies that no longer exist.

lore: Gar’Nok hails from the war torn lands of Grosh-Nak, where Orcs value strength, silence, and the ability to glare meaningfully at enemies until they run away. He grew up unsophisticated, barbaric, and violent, which made him perfectly normal by Orcish standards. What set him apart was a secret love of poetry, which he guarded more carefully than his favourite axe.

After a long day of slaughter, Gar’Nok likes to unwind with a few verses that combine heartfelt longing with enthusiastic destruction. He was thrilled when he discovered that ‘burning’ rhymes with ‘yearning’, because before that he had been pairing ‘burning’ with ‘killing’, which really limited his artistic range and held him back. Sadly, potential Orcish partners do not prefer the strong poetic type, which leaves him rather gloomy.

All this makes Gar'Nok rather sad, which is not good because Orcs have a proverb: 'If you feel sad, try a little murder'. As a poet, with his emotions running deep, Gar’Nok feels sadness more keenly than most. As a consequence though, when he tries a little murder, he also does it more violently than most. Hopefully once he figures out that ‘laughter’ doesn’t rhyme with ‘slaughter’ (even though it should!), he will calm down for a while and the killing will stop.

lore: The Dark Elves, by nature, are solitary creatures, not given to forming large cities or societies like the Humans or Dwarves of Krystara. Dokkalfar is typical of his kind - the fourth child of minor nobility. He had few prospects until he stumbled upon an ancient tome in a ruin predating the Dark Elves’ time in Zhul’Kari. The name of that tome was The Dark Swarm.

The Dark Swarm was in an ancient language. Dokkalfar traveled into Karakoth, where he studied that language until he could begin to decipher the book. It contained all manner of information about spiders - not just regular spiders though, many of the creatures on the tome’s pages came from distant dimensions beyond our own.

Eventually, Dokkalfar’s mastery of the tome, and the spells he found therein, was complete. He returned to Zhul’Kari, where his newfound knowledge proved useful as he murdered his way into the hierarchy of the corrupt Tower of Sorcery. To this day he jealously guards the tome, and few dare to interrupt his deeper studies as he scours its pages for more terrible secrets.

lore: In the dimensions beyond Krystara live many strange and powerful elder beings, whose names, thoughts, and motivations are incomprehensible to the ordinary folk of Krystara. Cthyryzyx is one of the lesser of these beings, but is still powerful and dangerous by mortal standards.

Born from the primordial ooze of the elder dimension, Cthyryzyx was summoned to Krystara by a Warlock in the mountains of Karakoth, looking to strike a bargain with an elder creature. Unfortunately, the Warlock’s circle of protection was incomplete, and one of Cthyryzyx’s tentacles snaked through, skewering the hapless Warlock through the eye.

Since then, Cthyryzyx has wandered the wastelands of Karakoth, looking for a portal back to his dimension. As he has no means to communicate with the Warlocks, his questions are misinterpreted as hostility, leading to attempts at binding spells, which in turn lead to more Warlocks losing an eye and one hemisphere of the brain behind it.

lore: Unlike most Centaurs of the Divinion Fields who grew up stargazing and debating philosophy, Bul'Tauros spent his childhood asking rocks if they had feelings, pretending they said yes, and then smashing them with his face. His father claimed he was descended from The Great Bull, his mother claimed the father was an idiot, and both were probably right.

Bul'Tauros is built like a siege engine with hooves and has the tactical subtlety of a dragon rolling down a hill. While other chieftains consult maps before a battle, Bul'Tauros prefers to charge in and yell at the terrain to fall into line. Surprisingly this works for him - in one battle, when the Dark Elves tried to outwit the Centaurs with clever formations and confusing banners, Bul'Tauros simply trampled through the middle and broke their strategy, their morale, several tents, and a few boulders that he insists told him they had feelings.

Despite this, he actually has a delicate hobby of carving tiny unicorns from the bones of his vanquished enemies, which he distributes to children with a grunt and a warning not to tell anyone. For example, after that Dark Elven battle, he gave a unicorn carving to the youngest surviving Dark Elven warrior and told her it was ‘for smashing well’. Nobody has ever corroborated that story though - nobody is foolish enough to do so.

lore: If you travel deep into the forests of Pan’s Vale, you might be unfortunate enough to encounter the Fey trickster known as Sylvasi. He tends to lurk in some of the darkest, most overgrown parts of the woods, just waiting for unwary travelers to pass by.  Frequently he’ll wait until they’re distracted or asleep before he pounces.

Sylvasi seldom kills his prey. He delights in a form of mischief that is more cruel than a swift death from his double blades could ever be; he likes to steal your weapons. By itself, that is ill-mannered and simply rude, but once you’re unarmed, he will climb up into the trees and make a racket to summon the less subtle creatures of the Vale. He then watches the carnage with pure delight.

Many folks wonder where Sylvasi came from, and why he acts like this. It is most likely he is simply an unwanted Fey child, abandoned at birth and now acting out with the unfettered mischievous nature of his people. One thing is for certain though, it’s wise to heed the old adage as you travel through Pan’s Vale: Keep your sword close, and stay in the light.

lore: Emperina was already old and wise when the Mines of Khaziel were nothing more than a few cosy tunnels she called home. As the Dwarves dug deeper and wider, her lair shrank smaller and smaller until she was left with a hidey-hole barely big enough for a dragon with any dignity. Rather than argue with an entire kingdom of miners, she simply left for a few centuries to cool off.

Emperina is patient, which is rare among Dragons. Over the centuries she waited out cave ins, mining booms, and even the occasional Dwarven singing festival without losing her temper. So she used her multi-century sabbatical to travel the lands of Krystara, reengaging with its peoples. She is a Dragon though, so reengaging varies in meaning from ‘sitting down for a nice tea and chat’ to ‘burning a village and eating its mayor’. She is basically nice, but draconic niceness knows its limits.

Eventually though, she returned to find a Daemon squatting in the mines and the Dwarves in desperate need of help. With some aid, she drove the creature out, reclaimed her space, and negotiated an uneasy truce. Now she lives beside the Dwarves in relative harmony; provided they do not mine her cave, she does not snack on their miners.

lore: From a young age, Elwyn the Bard’s long flowing hair, deep soulful eyes, and complete lack of responsibility made everyone assume greatness was inevitable. Sadly he lacked both memory and motivation, managing to retain only the first four lines of any limerick and refusing to learn the last one on principle. After being expelled from Bard School for attempting to charm the Headmaster’s daughter, he set out into the world with nothing but his looks and a busted old lute.

He may only know four lines of any ballad, but he delivers those four lines with such smouldering passion that audiences briefly forget he has no idea what comes next. He strums his lute with dramatic flair, gazes meaningfully into the distance, and then panics when the fifth line refuses to appear in his head. Somehow this has become his signature style, and tavern patrons now cheer when he inevitably improvises something embarrassing.

In Elwyn’s most fortunate moment, he stumbled into a band of Heroes who mistook his dramatic gestures for genuine talent. They kept him around out of pity at first, then out of habit, and eventually because his eighty percent finished limericks proved oddly inspiring in the middle of battle. To this day he travels with them, contributing enthusiasm, hair flips, and exactly four lines of poetry at a time.

lore: There are many races of Dwarves in Krystara, and all of them have great crafting skills. Perhaps the most fine-tuned skills of all are those of the Tinker Dwarves such as Sparkgrinder. Tinker Dwarves can be found throughout Krystara, but the largest group of them live in Adana.

Sparkgrinder, like most of his kin, has a brilliant mind and cunning hands, tempered with no trace of common sense or morality whatsoever. Some of his inventions have been miraculous, while others have, at times, left him in breach of the law and in dire trouble with the Adanian College of Engineers.

Despite the trouble he has caused over his long lifespan, the Adanian college allows him to live in his private junkyard on the outskirts of the capital city of New Adania. Within that huge pile of scrap, he and his adopted human daughter, Ghiralee, can always be found working on some strange new project.

lore: There was once a noble who lived in the northeastern corner of Sword’s Edge, called Lord Ghuldor. An ambitious type with a flair for the dramatic, he expanded his lands over the mountains, fighting tribes of Wargare, and eventually established his own Kingdom which he named Ghulvania, proclaiming himself rather pompously, the King in Crimson. The problem was that he never TRULY conquered that land.

Many other creatures still lived high in the mountains - in particular something OLD that went by the name Draakulis. One night, it snuck into the now-King Ghuldor’s chambers and infected him with a terrible disease that left him hungry for blood. That blood sustained him, extending his life far beyond mortal years, but it also gradually transformed him into a servant of Draakulis.

The creature came to be known as the Crimson Bat. Not one to be forgotten, even as he was changing, Ghuldor commissioned a mighty temple to be built (the Crimson Temple, of course) and hidden away, where his subjects; children would be regularly delivered to slake his thirst for blood.

lore: The first records of Abhorath involve his summoning by the Warlock Grimgin the Optimistic who, true to his name, thought a roast suckling pig might be enough to coax the dark secrets of the universe from a Daemon Lord. Abhorath devoured, suckling pig, then Grimgin, half of his tower, and a curious donkey who was just passing by. Sadly, Warlocks just don’t know when to leave a hungry eldritch beast alone, and now the “Daemon was out of the Bag” as they say in Karakoth.

Subsequent summoning attempts have been equally unsuccessful. In the most spectacular fail to date, he managed to consume not only the Warlock and 1,000 sacrificial goats, but also a neighboring kingdom, and a small mountain. It is remembered as both the greatest defeat in Karakoth’s history, and a cautionary tale about portion control.

The truth is, Abhorath doesn’t have a lot of secrets to share; his main skill is hunger. He took a double specialization in it when he leveled up to Daemon Lord a couple of eons ago. He spends his centuries lounging around the eldritch dimensions waiting for summoning attempts and free snacks. The only words of wisdom he has ever uttered are ‘Always start with what’s closest and easiest to chew’.

lore: The Lava Worms of the Broken Spire were first discovered by a Dwarven King - Firefist of Karak Lorgrim  - who disturbed them while he was digging for fire rubies. This probably would have been his headlining achievement, except that he also managed to disturb Infernus, and that was what really got everyone’s attention.

Greatest of the Lava Worms though was Sheggra. Centuries old, she had spawned thousands of young wormlings over that time (or Pyggrae as they were better known). Many of those she devoured, but many more went on to become great Lava Worms in their own right - some even swam through the deep lava tunnels to inhabit volcanoes on the mainland.

It was always rumored that the heart of a Lava Worm could melt the poison or disease from a mortal’s body. This was put to the test by General Luther - when his Queen was struck down by a potent poison, he traveled to Broken Spire, and cut out Sheggra’s heart to cure his beloved monarch. But Lava Worms have more than one heart…

lore: Frost Giants are not known for their incredible grasp on polite civility. But, every so often, a Frost Giant is born who is so unhinged and violent that his career choices are limited to one thing: Berserker. Even other Frost Giants - a generally disagreeable folk - will avoid disputes with their mad kinsfolk.

Once a Frost Giant is identified as a violent axe-murdering maniac, conventional Stormheim wisdom is to ship them as far north as possible to the kingdom of Hyndla Frostcrown, where their savage tendencies are honed by the Berserker King, Grimborn Bloodeye.

Grimborn’s Berserkers are mercenaries, available to any Giant clan who can meet their price. Unfortunately their method of pricing is as inconsistent as their warriors. It might range from a thousand barrels of ale, to a rare magical artifact, depending on Grimborn’s mood at the time.

lore: Dryads can be found in many forests throughout Krystara, even as far as the Underworld. Each Dryad has a tree to which she is bound. Dryads live for many centuries - their existence is tied to their tree, though they can exist outside of it for a time.

Often, when older Dryads have talked with their tree for centuries, it slowly becomes sentient and is known as a Treant. Many of the trees in the Forest of Thorns are over a thousand years old, they have been awake for centuries - they can move and converse quite freely.

On rare occasions a Dryad may leave her tree. This can be traumatic for both the tree and the Dryad, and the tree will often rot and die. If, on the other hand, a Dryad’s tree is cut down, she must find a new tree, or she will surely wither away.
